subject: jukebox
pitch: A 1950s diner jukebox. A tall rounded arch of glowing coloured tubes in red, amber and teal, chrome trim everywhere, a domed glass window showing a stack of records and the arm that picks them, rows of chrome selection buttons with little title cards, a speaker grille with a starburst pattern, and a coin slot.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a 1950s Wurlitzer-style jukebox prop built with the SDK, using a single root joint since it just needs a basic skeleton rather than multiple articulated parts.

Scaling to roughly 1.55m tall, 0.85m wide, 0.65m deep, facing +Z, I'm laying out the front: a chrome kickplate base, a lower cabinet with a starburst speaker grille, a middle control panel with buttons and coin slot, and an upper domed glass window showing a record stack and picker arm, framed by glowing colored tube arches in red, amber, and teal running down the sides as pilasters.

I'm settling on a color palette for the jukebox: a warm cabinet tone (leaning toward deep cherry or cream) paired with chrome trim faked through countershading—lighter metallic tones up top fading to darker shades below to simulate reflections. The glowing arch tubes in red, amber, and teal will sit against this cabinet body, similar to the classic Wurlitzer 1015 look.

Since there's no true emissive material available, I'll simulate the "glowing" effect using bright saturated colors against the dark fascia to create visual contrast instead.

Now I'm planning the geometry layout, setting the origin and depth dimensions, and thinking through the joint hierarchy for animated parts like the tonearm and turntable.

I'll add a few joints beyond root — a pickerPivot and pickerArm for the record picker mechanism — keeping it minimal but functional. I'm defining a helper function to simplify attaching parts to the root bone with position and rotation options, then moving on to building the cabinet body as an extruded front silhouette along the X and Y axes, pushed into depth along Z.

I'm thinking the cabinet should follow the classic Wurlitzer 1015 look with a rounded dome top — so I'll extrude the arch profile all the way through the depth rather than just capping the front, then figure out how the window and sloped control area recess into that shape.

Now I'm planning the layered front elements: a chrome-framed grille with a gold cloth starburst pattern (SVG texture with radiant rays in contrasting colors plus a central chrome emblem), sitting below the main window area.

Then I'm figuring out the sloped control deck below the window—a cream panel with chrome trim tilted back about 18°, built as a wedge-shaped extrusion to hold the button rows and title cards.

I'm thinking a slightly tilted near-vertical panel reads better from the front and 3/4 views than a fully horizontal shelf, so I'll place the buttons using a local coordinate frame oriented to the panel's normal and up vector.

I'll use ray-casting against the deck surface to seat the buttons exactly flush with the slanted face, then build each button as a chrome base ring plus a cap — laying out two rows of ten like classic jukebox selector buttons.

Next to each button I want a small title card: a textured cream rectangle with a colored stripe and fake text lines, giving the impression of song listings without needing actual readable text. I'm sketching the overall deck layout now — roughly 0.78 wide by 0.3 tall — trying to work out how the title-card strip and button columns should be arranged for a believable, readable composition.

Working through the vertical layout, I'm planning two rows of title cards (10 columns each) stacked above two rows of chrome selection buttons, with a coin mechanism plate near the bottom center. I'm also considering adding a volume knob, a coin-return cup, and a lit "NOW PLAYING" bar for extra detail, and figuring out how each button (with its chrome ring and cap) will be constructed as a multi-part object.

Now I'm shifting to the upper arch section of the cabinet, defining the glowing tube arrangement around the dome window and sketching the arch geometry centered above the deck — building the window as a rectangular base rising into a semicircular arch with a bulging glass dome in front.

Since materials here are opaque flat colors with no true transparency, I realize the dome glass can't be rendered as real see-through glass — instead I could fake it with a textured shell using alpha cutoff, where only reflection streaks and rim highlights are opaque and the rest is cut away so the records inside remain visible through the "glass."

Then I'd add a chrome bezel ring tracing the arch edge for the glazing frame, maybe with thin crossing strips to suggest glazing bars, while keeping the streaked glass shell front-facing only since the window is viewed head-on. For the interior, I need a dark recessed fascia behind the window so the records read as sitting inside a shadowed cavity, with the record items placed just in front of the solid body's back face so they're visible through the window opening.

I realize the depth layering needs rethinking: rather than one solid extruded body, I should split the cabinet into a rear solid shell (ending around z=0.04, forming the window's back wall) and a separate front facade built from side pillars and an arch-shaped sweep that frames the window hole, since a single extrusion can't easily produce a hole in the front face.

For the arch ring itself, I'm working out the sweep orientation — defining the path's up-vector so the section's radial half-width (rx) stays in-plane while the depth half (ry) points along world +Z, then laying out the arch path as straight sides rising up and curving over the top between roughly x=-0.34 and x=0.34.

I'm planning to sample the arc finely, every 10 degrees or so, to keep the corners between straight segments and curve tangent-continuous, likely feeding the point array through a catmull interpolation for smoothness. I'm sketching a reusable helper that builds an arch path from half-width, base height, and center height, generating the straight uprights plus arc samples swept from one side to the other.

Now I'm working out the depth layering: the body shell spans roughly -0.3 to 0.3 in z, with the lower cabinet section extruded as a rectangle at full depth and width, and the upper arch section sitting at the same front plane to form the facade with a window recess behind it.

For the facade itself, I'm placing the outer glowing ring as a radial box-section around the window opening, offset forward at z≈0.175, with the window cavity going deeper (z 0.05–0.3) to hold the visible mechanism — recalling that classic Wurlitzer jukeboxes show the turntable and record mechanism through that window, so I need that depth to feel believable rather than flat.

I'm deciding to model a stack of records standing vertically in a rack along X, like the Seeburg magazine style, using discs sized to 7-inch 45rpm records (radius ~0.089, thickness ~0.004) arranged in a row of 16 so the picker arm mechanism makes visual sense through the dome.

Actually, I think face-on discs read more instantly as "records" than an edge-on spindle stack would — a cascade of black discs with different colored labels, each offset slightly, feels like the clearer visual choice over a flat horizontal changer stack.

Actually, maybe a real record-changer setup works better: a spindle stack of discs on the left viewed slightly from above so their edges show as a striped column, paired with a chrome tonearm pivoting from the right that reaches over to a turntable with a single record playing — more like an actual mechanism than an abstract fan of discs.

I'm planning the window's interior backdrop — a warm amber-to-deep-red gradient on the back wall to simulate internal lamp glow, with a chrome mechanism base beneath it. Then I'm working out the arch geometry: window opening dimensions, cabinet silhouette radius, and the facade ring width surrounding the window.

Now I'm fitting three concentric colored tube arches (teal, amber, red) into that ring, separating them with thin chrome ribs and bezels, and adjusting the cabinet's half-width outward to give each tube enough room without feeling cramped.

I'm deciding on color order — red outermost, amber middle, teal innermost against the dark window — and figuring out how the tubes extend down the sides as vertical pilasters, ending with chrome caps and possibly a chrome footing bar closing the arch under the window.

Now I'm working out how to sweep the colored arch tubes as round-profile paths with highlight stripes, and puzzling through how the stripe orientation should flip depending on whether a given leg runs up or down.

Working through the vector algebra, I find that once the tube tilts even slightly from vertical, the "0" reference direction becomes the outward radial direction of the arch rather than staying tied to the front normal — so the projection of world-up perpendicular to the tangent naturally sweeps from front-facing to outward-facing as the path curves, giving continuity without a discontinuous jump.

Actually there's a discontinuity risk between the leg and arch conventions, so instead of relying on angular sectors I could paint the highlight directly based on surface normal direction—wherever the normal's Z component is high, that's the front-facing stripe, which sidesteps the clock-angle ambiguity entirely and should read as a soft, correctly-placed highlight regardless of tube segment.

I'm checking that the painted texel density stays reasonable across the ~0.5m² of tube surface, and planning to budget total painted area (tubes, wood grain, grille cloth) against the flat-colour atlas so density doesn't suffer. For the neon glow itself, I'd blend from a dark tube colour to a bright core using the normal's Z value, with a near-white highlight where the surface faces almost directly forward, though I still need to account for how the light direction affects shading on top of that.

Thinking through visibility, the front-facing stripe approach works fine for the vertical legs and the arch top since both face forward, while back-facing surfaces simply won't be seen, so a uniform paint rule across all tube segments should hold up. I also want to add chrome collar caps at the base of each tube and continue the design with a decorative chrome crest or sunburst ornament at the top of the arch for that 1950s styling.

I'm planning chrome trim details: a box-section strip along the arch's outer edge, a row of tiny chrome studs for bolts, and a nameplate with a made-up brand name like "STARLITE" rendered in a bold sans-serif SVG text, plus smaller labels like "SELECT RECORD" and a coin slot marked "PLAY 5¢" on the deck.

I'm also sketching the lower cabinet: a starburst speaker grille with a chrome frame and corner bars, a kick-plate base with stubby feet, vertical go-faster chrome strips on the mahogany sides, a coin slot plate with a dark slot, return cup, and red button, and considering whether a small curled power cord at the back is worth the detail since it won't really be visible.

Writing SVG rays...

I need everything opaque since low-alpha strokes get cut from the texture, so I'll use solid darker colors instead of transparency for the cloth-weave slat lines, maybe adding tiny perforation dots at a fine pitch, and sizing the grille texture around 768px to match its 1.9375 aspect ratio. Now I'm shifting to the window mechanism geometry, starting with the opening's half-width and bottom position.

I'm laying out the vertical bands — deck, nameplate area, and lower grille — then starting to place the interior mechanism elements like a floor shelf and spindle-mounted record stack inside the window opening.

For the records themselves, I'm sizing a stack of about 16 discs with thin pitch so they read as visible layers, debating whether to vary the rim colors between black and other hues so the edges are distinguishable from the front view since the labels on top wouldn't be visible from that angle.

Now I'm designing a second record spinning on an active turntable platter positioned to the side of the stack, with its own spindle and red label, plus working out a picker arm mechanism that would swing from a rear pivot to lift the top record off the stack and transfer it to the platter, though the geometry feels a bit cramped at this scale.

Checking that the arch narrows toward the top, I'll keep the stack, picker arm, and lifted record below y~1.13 to stay safe. I'm working out the facade structure more carefully: the arch-shaped ring needs vertical legs extending down to meet a horizontal nameplate band below the window, while the lower deck wedge sits further down still.
